items.setup: A client two weeks into a new exercise routine
items.quote: I skipped Tuesday, so the whole month is blown. I might as well stop.
items.why: One missed day puts the entire month in the failure category. Nothing partial is available, only intact or ruined.

items.setup: A client describing a first date
items.quote: Either he's the one or the whole evening was a waste.
items.why: Two categories with nothing between them. An evening that was pleasant but not life-changing has nowhere to land.

items.setup: A graduate student after a group presentation
items.quote: I stumbled on one slide. Either you can present or you can't, and clearly I can't.
items.why: The client names two fixed categories and sorts into one. Labeling would stop at the identity claim; here the either/or structure is what produces it.

items.setup: A client after a second unsuccessful job interview
items.quote: That's twice now. I never get past a first interview.
items.why: Two instances become never. The tell is an absolute quantifier resting on a very small sample.

items.setup: A client whose neighbor did not wave back
items.quote: Nobody in this building has any interest in knowing me.
items.why: One non-event expands to everyone in the building. Mind reading would be a claim about what the neighbor was thinking; this is a claim about how many people feel it.

items.setup: A client describing their marriage after an argument
items.quote: Every conversation we have turns into this.
items.why: Every does the work. A mental filter would mean the client is only noticing the arguments; here they assert there is nothing else to notice.

items.setup: A client describing four days with extended family
items.quote: Four days together and all I can think about is the twenty minutes my brother and I argued.
items.why: The negative twenty minutes crowds out the other four days. Discounting the positive would mean explaining the good days away; here they simply drop out of view.

items.setup: A client reviewing written feedback on a paper
items.quote: There were three positives and one criticism. I've read the criticism nine times.
items.why: Attention keeps returning to the single negative item while the three positives go unread. The ratio the client reports is the giveaway.

items.setup: A client who received a thank-you card from someone they helped
items.quote: Anyone would have gotten a card. It doesn't mean I did anything for her.
items.why: The evidence is admitted and then neutralized, so it cannot update the client's view of their own competence.

items.setup: A client praised by name in a staff meeting
items.quote: My supervisor has to say things like that. It's her job.
items.why: The praise is reframed as an obligation rather than a judgment, which strips its value as evidence.

items.setup: A client whose friend has not replied in two days
items.quote: She's annoyed with me. I can tell.
items.why: A specific mental state is attributed to another person and treated as known. Fortune telling would predict an event rather than report someone's present thoughts.

items.setup: A client describing an interview panel
items.quote: The one on the left had already decided against me before I sat down.
items.why: The interviewer's private conclusion is reported as fact, with no evidence offered for it.

items.setup: A client after a family gathering
items.quote: They were all thinking I'd put on weight. Nobody said it, but they were thinking it.
items.why: The client notes the absence of evidence out loud and keeps the conclusion anyway, which is the clearest form of this one.

items.setup: A client considering a return to school
items.quote: I'd drop out by October. I know how it would go.
items.why: A future outcome is stated as already known, then used to close the question before it is examined.

items.setup: A client invited to a friend's wedding
items.quote: I'll stand in the corner all night and nobody will talk to me.
items.why: The client narrates an event that has not happened. Mind reading would be a claim about what the other guests currently think of them.

items.setup: A client who was passed over for a promotion last year
items.quote: I'm not going to get it. I already know how this ends.
items.why: A specific future outcome is stated as already known and settled, closing off the question before it is examined. There is no cascade of consequences — just the prediction itself, treated as fact.

items.setup: A client who found an unexplained charge on a credit card
items.quote: If this is fraud, they'll drain the account, we'll miss rent, and we'll be out by the first.
items.why: A chain of escalating consequences is built from one uncertain event, each link treated as automatically following the last.

items.setup: A social work intern before a supervision meeting
items.quote: If this goes badly, I'll be put on a performance plan, which means I'll be pulled from the placement, and then no program will take me after that.
items.why: One difficult meeting triggers a chain of escalating consequences, each presented as automatically following the last. Fortune telling would stop at a single predicted outcome; here every step is a new threshold crossed on the way to something worse.

items.setup: A client whose car made an unfamiliar noise
items.quote: It's the transmission. That's four thousand dollars, which means no car, which means I lose the job.
items.why: One sound becomes a cascade ending in job loss, with no step along the way treated as uncertain.

items.setup: A client describing a decision they made at work
items.quote: It feels like the wrong call, so it was the wrong call.
items.why: The feeling is the only evidence offered, and it is treated as settling a question of fact.

items.setup: A client asked to lead a project at work
items.quote: I'm terrified, and you don't get that scared about something you can actually do.
items.why: Fear is converted into evidence of incapacity. The emotion does the work a fact would normally have to do.

items.setup: A client in their first semester of a graduate program
items.quote: I feel like a fraud in there, which tells me I don't belong.
items.why: The feeling is read as information about reality — the emotion itself is the evidence. Mind reading would be a claim about what classmates currently think; mental filter would mean fixating on one negative moment while the rest fades.

items.setup: A client three weeks after their mother's funeral
items.quote: I ought to be functioning by now.
items.why: A rule about the correct pace of grief is applied to the client's own experience, and the gap becomes a personal shortcoming.

items.setup: A client describing their role as the oldest sibling
items.quote: I'm supposed to hold this family together. That's the job.
items.why: An unexamined obligation is stated as fact. Personalization would assign blame for an outcome; here the client is naming a standing duty.

items.setup: A client whose adult daughter rarely calls
items.quote: A daughter should call her mother. That is how it works.
items.why: A rule about how another person must behave, with the distress arising from the violation rather than from the event itself.

items.setup: A client who forgot a coworker's name
items.quote: I'm just an idiot. That's all there is to it.
items.why: A single lapse becomes a fixed global identity. The move is from a thing that happened to a noun about the self.

items.setup: A client describing a former partner
items.quote: He's a narcissist. That explains all of it.
items.why: A person is reduced to a category that then substitutes for explanation. This one applies to other people as readily as to the self.

items.setup: A client who cried during a work presentation
items.quote: Now I'm the weak one in that office.
items.why: One moment becomes a permanent identity. Mind reading would be a claim about what coworkers currently think; this is a claim about who the client now is.

items.setup: A client whose team lost a long-standing contract
items.quote: If I had caught that error, we'd still have them.
items.why: Sole responsibility is taken for a multi-causal outcome, with everyone else's contribution absent from the account.

items.setup: A parent whose child is struggling in school
items.quote: This is on me. I should have read to her more when she was little.
items.why: The client names themselves as the cause of an outcome with many contributors. The should clause is the mechanism; the causal claim is the distortion.
